blocks.text: INTRODUCTION

The trachea and bronchi are cartilaginous and membranous air conduits intended to convey the respiratory current. The trachea is an airy, odd and median fibro-cartilaginous conduit, following the larynx at the level of the 6th cervical vertebra and ending in the thorax at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra by bifurcating into 02 main bronchi (stem bronchi). There are two portions: The cervical portion, superficial, extends from the lower edge of the cricoid cartilage to the upper edge of the sternal manubrium. The deep thoracic portion extends from the base of the neck to the 5th thoracic vertebra. Obstruction of the trachea can be fatal. Bronchial fibroscopy allows easy exploration of the trachea and bronchi. INTRODUCTION The trachea and bronchi are cartilaginous and membranous air tubes designed to carry the respiratory flow. The trachea is an odd, median, fibro-cartilaginous air tube, which follows the larynx at the level of the 6th cervical vertebra and ends in the thorax at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra, bifurcating into 02 main bronchi (stem bronchi). It has two distinct portions: The superficial cervical portion extends from the lower edge of the cricoid cartilage to the upper edge of the sternal manubrium. The deep thoracic portion extends from the base of the neck to the 5th thoracic vertebra. Obstruction of the trachea can be fatal. Bronchial fibroscopy allows easy exploration of the trachea and bronchi.

blocks.text: THE TRACHEA

It follows the larynx and is divided into two bronchi: the main bronchi. The trachea, obstructed by a foreign body or a piece of food that has gone the wrong way, can be a cause of sudden death. The Heimlich maneuver allows this foreign body to be expelled urgently. Indeed, the brutal compressure of the epigastrium raises the diaphragm, and promotes the emission of residual air which expels the foreign body. DESCRIPTIVE ANATOMY Origin: It arises at the lower edge of the cricoid cartilage, at the height of the 6th cervical vertebra (C6). Course and direction: It descends almost vertically, in front of the esophagus, slightly behind and to the right.

items: Cervical approach: in the middle and lower part of the neck.
Then thoracic: in the upper part of the thorax.
Termination: opposite the T4-T5 intervertebral disc

Shape and dimensions: It is a cylindrical tube flattened on its posterior face. It is elastic and measures in adults approximately 11cm in length and 20mm in transverse diameter. The anterior part has 15 to 20 transverse projections corresponding to the cartilaginous rings, separated by inter-annular depressures. The posterior part, musculo-aponeurotic, is flat. It has 2 lateral depressures on its left side:
At the top, the thyroid imprint at the level of the left lobe.
Below, the aortic impressure.

blocks.text: MEANS OF FIXITY: The cervical trachea is held in place by its continuity with the larynx and by its adhesion with the esophagus and the thyroid body. The thoracic trachea is held in place by its continuity with the cervical trachea, the larynx and its adherence to the esophagus and the arch of the aorta. The trachea is relatively mobile, it descends during inspiration and rises again during expiration. INTERIOR CONFIGURATION Pink in color, it has annular projections, and at the level of the tracheal bifurcation, a sagittal crest: the carina of the trachea (or the carina).

REPORTS 1- THE CERVICAL PORTION: it is contained, with the esophagus, in the visceral sheath of the neck. Previous reports: It responds to the isthmus of the thyroid gland which covers the 2nd, 3rd and 4th tracheal cartilages, the superior and middle thyroid arteries, the brachiocephalic trunk, the inferior thyroid veins and the thymus. Superficially. It is covered by the sternothyroid, sternohyoid muscles and the pretracheal blade of the cervical fascia, the skin and the subcutaneous cellular tissuee. Posterior reports: Responds to the esophagus in the same visceral sheath, overflowing the trachea on the left, accompanied on each side by the recurrent nerve. Laterally: It is related to the thyroid lobes, in the visceral sheath; and with the jugulo-carotid bundle, made up of: the primary carotid, the internal jugular and the pneumogastric. This bundle is accompanied by the jugular lymphatic chain, outside the visceral sheath.

blocks.text: 3- TRACHEAL BIFURCATION The trachea is divided, at the level of the T4-T5 intervertebral disc, into 2 bronchi: the main or main bronchi, right and left. The 2 bronchi move apart at an angle of approximately 70° and are joined by the inter-bronchial ligament. Relations of the tracheal bifurcation: In front: The arch of the aorta, the right branch of the pulmonary artery, the superior vena cava more to the right. The cardiac ganglia of (Wrisberg); further to the left, and the thymus; further forward. Behind: The esophagus and the thoracic duct. Top right: the cross of the azygos vein. On the left: the arch of the aorta. Bottom: The bifurcation of the pulmonary artery, the intertracheobronchial nodes and the left atrium.

blocks.text: THE BRONCHES

These are semi-rigid arborescent air ducts located between the trachea and the alveoli. They divide into lobar bronchi which are subdivided into segmental bronchi. The latter branch into bronchioles. The main bronchi have 2 segments: An extra-pulmonary segment and an intra-pulmonary segment which is part of the constitution of the lung. They have the same structure as the trachea. The right main bronchus or right main bronchus Almost vertical, short, concave medially, measures approximately 2 to 2.5 cm in length and 12 to 14 mm in diameter. Its orientation explains the frequency of passage of foreign bodies to the right. It gives 03 lobar bronchi: The right upper lobar bronchus: which is divided into: apical or superior segmental bronchus, the dorsal or posterior segmental bronchus, and the ventral or anterior segmental bronchus. The right middle lobar bronchus: is divided into: lateral or external segmental bronchus and medial or internal segmental bronchus. The right lower lobar bronchus: branches into: apical or superior segmental bronchus or Nelson's bronchus, mid-basal or paracardiac or internal basal segmental bronchus, venro-basal or anterior basal segmental bronchus, latero-basal or external basal segmental bronchus, and finally end-basal or posterior basal segmental bronchus. b. The left main bronchus or left main bronchus: Oblique, longer (approximately 5cm in length and 9 to 11 mm in diameter), presents 2 curvatures: first concave outwards and upwards, near its origin, due to the presence of the arch of the aorta. Lower down, it is concave inward and downward, responding to the convexity of the heart. Its endoscopic exploration is sometimes difficult. It ends in 2 lobar bronchi: upper and lower.

items: A cranial trunk which is subdivided into apico-posterior and anterior segmental bronchi

A caudal trunk which is subdivided into superior and inferior segmental lingular bronchi. The left lower lobar bronchus: has the same layout as its right counterpart, the only difference being the birth, through a common trunk, of the 2 segmental bronchi: the ventro-basal and the paracardiac. All the segmental bronchi divide into subsegmental bronchi which divide in turn, and their final bronchial branches, called supralobular bronchi, lead to the pulmonary lobules. Each sublobular bronchus enters the lobule and is called the intralobular bronchus. The latter divides 5 to 6 times in a row and the last branches are called terminal bronchioles. Each terminal bronchiole widens and becomes a bumpy conduit: the alveolar canal, which undergoes a certain number of divisions, forming a bouquet of canals covered with bumps called the alveoli.

Abstract The trachea and bronchi are part of the respiratory system that plays a vital role in the respiratory system by conducting air to and from the lungs.

items: The trachea is a flexible, tube-like structure approximately 10–12 cm in length and 2–2.5 cm in diameter. It is located in front of the esophagus, extending from the larynx to the point where it divides into two bronchi at the carina.The tracheal wall is composed of Cartilaginous rings, 16–20 C-shaped cartilage rings keep the trachea open, allowing air to flow. The open part of the ring faces the esophagus.
The trachea bifurcates into the right and left main bronchi at the level of the carina, a ridge of cartilage.

items: The main bronchi have a structure similar to the trachea, with cartilage and smooth muscle, but as they branch into smaller airways, the amount of cartilage decreases.
Each main bronchius divides into lobar bronchi, which corresponds to the lobes of the lungs:

blocks.text: o Right lung has three lobar bronchi: upper, middle, and lower. o Left lung has two lobar bronchi: upper and lower

items: The lobar bronchi further divide into segmental bronchi, which supply specific bronchopulmonary segments within the lobes of the lungs. There are 10 segments in each lung.

The segmental bronchi branch into smaller bronchioles, which lack cartilage and are primarily composed of smooth muscle. Bronchioles continue to branch into terminal bronchioles and then into respiratory bronchioles, which connect to the alveolar ducts leading to the alveoli (air sacs where gas exchange occurs).
